q: Electricity is a form of energy.
e: Electricity is fundamentally a form of energy that can be transformed into other forms such as heat, mechanical, light, and sound energy.

q: There are two types of electricity: electrostatics and electrodynamics.
e: The two types of electricity are electrostatics (static electricity) and electrodynamics (current electricity).

q: Electrostatics is the study of moving electric charges and their interaction with magnetic and electric fields.
e: Electrostatics is the study of electric charge at rest. Electrodynamics is the study of moving electric charges.

q: Electric charge is the physical property of matter that causes an electric force when placed in an electromagnetic field.
e: This is the exact definition of electric charge as a physical property of matter.

q: Electric charges may be either at rest (static charges) or in motion (moving charges).
e: Electric charges can exist in a state of rest, known as static charges, or in motion, known as moving charges.

q: Flow of charges is called an electric field.
e: The flow of charges is called an electric current, not an electric field.

q: A French scientist, Du Fay, studied the nature of electric charges possessed by substances and found that there were only two kinds of charges.
e: Du Fay discovered that there are only two kinds of electric charges possessed by substances.

q: Benjamin Franklin named the two kinds of charges positive charge and negative charge.
e: Benjamin Franklin is credited with naming the two kinds of charges positive and negative.

q: Positive charge is represented by a minus sign (-).
e: Positive charge is represented by a plus sign (+), while negative charge is represented by a minus sign (-).

q: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
e: This is a fundamental principle of electrostatics: like charges repel each other, and unlike charges attract each other.

q: The closer the charges are, the greater the force between them.
e: The electric force between two charged objects increases as the distance between them decreases.

q: When two charged objects are brought together, they produce either attractive or repulsive force.
e: Depending on whether the charges are like or unlike, the resulting force will be either repulsive or attractive.

q: The electric force between two charged objects is one of the fundamental forces of nature.
e: The electric force is recognized as one of the fundamental forces of nature.

q: The electric force holds the particles that make up a molecule together.
e: The electric force holds the particles that make up an atom together, not specifically a molecule.

q: Charged objects can exert forces to other charged objects without being in contact with them.
e: Charged objects can exert forces on each other at a distance without physical contact.

q: This is possible because there is a magnetic field around each charge.
e: This is possible because there is an electric field around each charge, not a magnetic field.

q: In SI units, electric charge is measured in coulomb (C).
e: The SI unit for measuring electric charge is the coulomb (C).

q: The unit coulomb is in honour of Charles Augustin de Coulomb, a French physicist.
e: The coulomb is named after the French physicist Charles Augustin de Coulomb.

q: Coulomb discovered that the force between two charged objects depends on the magnitude of their charges and on how far apart they are.
e: Coulomb's discovery established that electric force depends on both charge magnitude and distance.

q: The magnitude of charge of an electron is $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.
e: The fundamental charge of a single electron is exactly $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.

q: One coulomb of charge is equivalent to the charge of $6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons.
e: Since one electron has a charge of $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C, one coulomb equals the charge of $6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons.

q: One coulomb is a relatively small value of charge.
e: One coulomb is a relatively large value of charge in the context of electrostatics.

q: 1 microcoulomb ($1 \mu$C) is equal to $10^{-6}$ C.
e: One microcoulomb is one millionth of a coulomb, which is $10^{-6}$ C.

q: Charge is one of the quantized physical quantities.
e: Electric charge is quantized, meaning it exists only in discrete, indivisible units.

q: Charge can take any arbitrary values.
e: Charge cannot take any arbitrary values; it can only take discrete values that are integral multiples of the fundamental charge.

q: Charge can only take discrete values that are integral multiples of the fundamental charge.
e: This is the definition of charge quantization, where the fundamental charge is the charge of an electron.

q: The formula for quantized charge is $Q = ne$, where $n$ is an integer.
e: In the equation $Q = ne$, $Q$ is the electric charge, $n$ is an integer, and $e$ is the charge of an electron.

q: Matter is composed of atoms which are very small in size.
e: All matter is fundamentally composed of extremely small particles called atoms.

q: An atom consists of a core called the nucleus around which the particles called protons are moving in orbits.
e: An atom consists of a nucleus around which the particles called electrons are moving in orbits.

q: An electron is a negatively charged particle having a charge of $-1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.
e: The electron carries a negative charge with a magnitude of $1.6 \times 10^{-19}$ C.

q: The nucleus consists of two kinds of particles called proton and neutron.
e: The atomic nucleus is composed of positively charged protons and uncharged neutrons.

q: A proton is a positively charged particle and a neutron is an uncharged particle.
e: Protons carry a positive charge, while neutrons have no electric charge.

q: An electron and a proton have the same magnitude of electric charge.
e: Although their signs are opposite, the magnitude of the charge of an electron and a proton is identical.

q: The nucleus has net negative charge.
e: The nucleus has a net positive charge due to the presence of protons.

q: The magnitude of positive charge of the nucleus is equal to the sum of the positive charges of all the protons present in the nucleus.
e: The total positive charge of the nucleus is the sum of the charges of all its constituent protons.

q: In a normal atom the number of orbiting electrons is always equal to the number of protons.
e: A normal, uncharged atom maintains an equal number of protons and electrons.

q: Since the magnitude of positive charge of the nucleus is equal to that of the total negative charge of electrons, a normal atom has no net charge.
e: The equal and opposite charges of protons and electrons cancel each other out, resulting in no net charge.

q: A normal atom is said to be electrically neutral.
e: Because it has no net electric charge, a normal atom is electrically neutral.

q: If an atom gains one or more electrons, it carries a positive charge.
e: If an atom gains one or more electrons, it carries a negative charge due to the excess of negative particles.

q: If an atom loses one or more electrons, it becomes positively charged.
e: Losing electrons leaves the atom with more protons than electrons, resulting in a net positive charge.

q: When an atom becomes a charged atom, it is called an ion.
e: A charged atom, whether positive or negative, is referred to as an ion.

q: In an atom the negatively charged electrons are moving around a positively charged nucleus.
e: Electrons, which are negatively charged, orbit the positively charged nucleus of an atom.

q: The electrons closer to the nucleus experience less attractive force of the nucleus.
e: The electrons closer to the nucleus experience a greater attractive force from the nucleus.

q: The electrons closer to the nucleus cannot move freely and are called bound electrons.
e: Due to the strong attractive force, inner electrons are tightly bound and cannot move freely.

q: The electrons far away from the nucleus are loosely bound and are called free electrons.
e: Outer electrons experience less attractive force, making them loosely bound and free to move.

q: Free electrons can move from one atom to another.
e: Because they are loosely bound, free electrons can transfer between atoms.

q: The number of free electrons in a substance depends upon the nature of that substance.
e: Different substances have different atomic structures, which determines the number of free electrons they possess.

q: The substance which has plenty of free electrons is called an insulator.
e: A substance with plenty of free electrons is called a conductor, not an insulator.

q: The substance which has very few or no free electrons is called an insulator.
e: Insulators lack free electrons, which prevents the easy flow of electric charge.

q: Metals are good electrical conductors.
e: Metals contain many free electrons, making them excellent conductors of electricity.

q: Most non-metals conduct electricity well, although carbon is an exception.
e: Most non-metals conduct electricity poorly or not at all, although carbon is an exception.

q: In insulators all the electrons are held tightly in position and unable to move from atom to atom.
e: The electrons in insulators are tightly bound to their atoms, preventing electrical conduction.

q: Although the electrons are not free to move in insulators, they can be transferred from one object to another.
e: While electrons cannot move freely within an insulator, they can be transferred between different objects, such as by rubbing.

q: Some substances which contain a moderate amount of free electrons are called semiconductors.
e: Semiconductors have an intermediate number of free electrons, placing them between conductors and insulators.

q: Semiconductors are both conductors and insulators.
e: Semiconductors are neither conductors nor insulators; they have properties distinct from both.

q: Silicon and germanium are widely used as semiconductors.
e: Silicon and germanium are the most common elements used in semiconductor technology.

q: Metals such as gold, silver, copper, brass, aluminium etc., are good conductors.
e: These metals are well-known for their high electrical conductivity due to abundant free electrons.

q: Non-metals such as plastic, glass, rubber, wax, quartz, etc., are insulators.
e: These non-metallic materials are classic examples of electrical insulators.

q: Transistors and other electronic components are made from semiconductors.
e: The semiconductor properties of materials like silicon are essential for manufacturing transistors and electronic components.

q: Normally, atoms have equal numbers of electrons and protons so the net charge on a material is zero.
e: In a neutral state, the equal number of protons and electrons results in a net charge of zero.

q: When two insulating materials are rubbed together, protons may be transferred from one to the other.
e: When two insulating materials are rubbed together, electrons may be transferred, not protons.

q: If two uncharged objects are rubbed with one another both of them become charged.
e: Rubbing two uncharged objects together causes electron transfer, leaving both objects charged.

q: Charging by rubbing is also called charging by friction.
e: The process of electrification by rubbing is commonly referred to as charging by friction.

q: Rubbing produces or creates new charges.
e: Rubbing does not produce or create charges; it only transfers existing electrons from one object to another.

q: When a glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth, the glass rod becomes positively charged.
e: The glass rod loses electrons to the silk cloth, resulting in a net positive charge on the glass rod.

q: When a glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth, the silk cloth becomes positively charged.
e: The silk cloth gains electrons from the glass rod, so it becomes negatively charged.

q: The glass rod becomes positively charged because it loses electrons.
e: The loss of negatively charged electrons leaves the glass rod with a net positive charge.

q: When a plastic rod is rubbed with fur, the plastic rod possesses a negative charge.
e: The plastic rod gains electrons from the fur, giving it a net negative charge.

q: When a plastic rod is rubbed with fur, the fur becomes negatively charged.
e: The fur loses electrons to the plastic rod, so the fur becomes positively charged.

q: Induction is the process of charging a conductor without any contact with the charged body.
e: Charging by induction involves redistributing charges in a conductor using a nearby charged object, without physical contact.

q: A charged object can attract uncharged objects.
e: A charged object can induce a charge separation in an uncharged object, leading to attraction.

q: When a negatively charged rod is placed near a metal sphere, like charges repel so electrons in the sphere move to the right side of the sphere.
e: The negative rod repels the free electrons in the metal sphere, pushing them to the far side.

q: When the sphere is touched by a wire connected to earth, electrons flow from the earth to the sphere.
e: When the sphere is earthed, electrons flow from the sphere to the earth, not from the earth to the sphere.

q: After the connection is removed and the charged object is taken away, the sphere becomes a positively charged object.
e: Because electrons flowed to the earth, the sphere is left with a deficit of electrons, making it positively charged.

q: Finally, the positive charges are uniformly distributed on the surface of the sphere.
e: Once the inducing charge is removed, the remaining positive charges spread out evenly over the sphere's surface.

q: Two metal spheres of the same size supported on insulating stands are in contact can be considered as a single conductor.
e: When in contact, the two metal spheres act together as one continuous conducting body.

q: When a negatively charged rubber rod is brought near sphere A, free electrons in both spheres move towards the rod.
e: Since like charges repel, the free electrons in both spheres move away from the negatively charged rod.

q: When a negatively charged rod is brought near, sphere A has excess positive charges, while sphere B has excess negative charges.
e: Electrons are repelled to sphere B, leaving sphere A with a deficit of electrons (positive) and sphere B with an excess (negative).

q: These excess charges on the surfaces of A and B are called induced charges.
e: The charges that appear on the surfaces of the spheres due to the nearby charged object are known as induced charges.

q: Keeping the rubber rod in position, sphere B moves slightly from sphere A, and the two spheres have opposite charges.
e: Separating the spheres while the rod is present traps the opposite charges on each respective sphere.

q: After the rubber rod is removed, sphere A becomes a negatively charged sphere.
e: After the rod is removed, sphere A remains a positively charged sphere because it lost electrons to sphere B.

q: Sphere A and B now have an equal number of opposite charges, and the magnitude of the charge on the rubber rod remains unchanged.
e: Induction does not transfer charge to or from the inducing rod, so its charge magnitude remains unchanged.

q: The law of conservation of electric charge is one of the fundamental laws.
e: The conservation of electric charge is a fundamental principle in physics.

q: The net electric charge in an isolated system remains constant.
e: This is the statement of the law of conservation of electric charge.

q: The net charge is the algebraic sum of the charges in an isolated system.
e: Net charge is calculated by adding all positive and negative charges algebraically within the system.

q: In the experiment on electrification by stroking the glass rod with a silk cloth, they together form an isolated system.
e: The glass rod and silk cloth together can be considered an isolated system where no charge enters or leaves.

q: There is charge transfer between the surrounding and the isolated system during stroking.
e: There is no charge transfer between the surrounding and the isolated system; charge is only transferred between the rod and the cloth.

q: Photocopier, electrostatic paint spraying, electrostatic precipitator etc., are based on static electric charges.
e: These are practical daily life applications that utilize the principles of static electricity.

q: Basic operation of a photocopier is the attraction of charged toner to the region on the selenium coated drum that is oppositely charged.
e: The photocopier works by using electrostatic attraction to pull charged toner onto specific oppositely charged areas of the drum.

q: In electrostatic paint spraying, the item to be painted receives the positive charge from a positively charged electrode.
e: In electrostatic paint spraying, the item to be painted receives a negative charge from a negatively charged electrode.

q: The droplets of paint emerge from the spray gun are positively charged.
e: The paint droplets are given a positive charge so they will be attracted to the negatively charged object.

q: As the paint droplets all carry the same charge they repel and spread out forming a fine spray.
e: Mutual repulsion between the positively charged droplets causes them to spread out evenly.

q: The paint is attracted statically to metal frame from every direction so there is no waste of spray paint.
e: The electrostatic attraction ensures the paint wraps around the frame, minimizing waste.

q: In an electrostatic precipitator, waste smoke, dust and fly ash are passed through a positively charged mesh of wire.
e: In an electrostatic precipitator, the waste smoke and ash are passed through a negatively charged mesh of wire.

q: In the chimney, the negatively charged fly ash particles are attracted and stick to positively charged metal plate.
e: The negatively charged ash particles are attracted to the oppositely charged (positive) collecting plates.

q: Static electricity occurs when there is an imbalance of charges between two objects.
e: An imbalance of positive and negative charges between objects is the scientific definition of static electricity.

q: Static electricity can build up as a result of collisions among the molecules in clouds.
e: Friction and collisions between molecules in clouds can generate a significant buildup of static charge.

q: A huge spark forming between the ground and the cloud causes a lightning discharge.
e: Lightning is a massive electrostatic discharge caused by the spark between a charged cloud and the ground.

q: As aircraft fly through the air, they can become charged with static electricity.
e: Friction with air molecules during flight can cause an aircraft to accumulate static electric charge.

q: A build-up of static charge is a potential danger when refuelling aircraft or vehicles.
e: Static charge buildup can create sparks, which is highly dangerous in the presence of flammable fuel.

q: Fuel running through the pipes can provide the friction needed to create a static charge.
e: The flow and friction of fuel inside pipes can generate static electricity.

q: To prevent static charge build-up, aircraft are earthed with an insulator during refuelling.
e: To prevent static charge build-up, aircraft are earthed with a conductor, not an insulator, during refuelling.

q: Fuel tankers that transport fuel on roads must be earthed before any fuel is transferred, to prevent sparks causing a fire or explosion.
e: Earthing the fuel tanker safely dissipates any static charge, preventing dangerous sparks.

q: Television screen and computer monitors become charged with static electricity when they are powered.
e: The operation of these electronic displays can lead to a buildup of static electric charge on their surfaces.

q: These static charges on screens attract dust.
e: The static charge on the screen attracts neutral dust particles from the surrounding air.
